regulation_content.regulation_text:
1. Short title and Commencement
(1) These regulations may be called the International Financial Services Centres Authority (Managing
General Agents) Regulations, 2026.
(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Names the instrument and sets when it takes effect. The regulations are cited as the IFSCA (Managing General Agents) Regulations, 2026 and come into force on the date of gazette publication, i.e. 12 June 2026.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Effective 12 Jun 2026 (gazette date)

regulation_content.regulation_text:
2. Objective
These regulations aims to provide a comprehensive regulatory framework for the registration, regulation and
operation of Managing General Agents (MGAs) operating in International Financial Services Centres (IFSCs)
in India, which possess delegated authority from the foreign insurer(s) for underwriting direct insurance
business or settlement of claims, ensuring they operate with transparency and accountability to protect
policyholders’ interests and support the orderly growth and development of the insurance ecosystem in the
IFSCs.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: States the purpose: a single registration-and-conduct framework for MGAs in IFSCs that hold delegated authority from foreign insurers to underwrite direct insurance business or settle claims, with policyholder protection and orderly market development as the stated aims.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The objective clause frames the two pillars every later provision serves — delegated authority exercised for a foreign insurer, and protection of the policyholder who sits behind that insurer. When a later provision reads ambiguously, this dual purpose is the interpretive anchor the Authority will fall back on.

regulation_content.regulation_text:
3. Definitions
(1) For the purposes of these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires, the terms defined herein
shall bear the meanings as assigned to them below, and their cognate expressions shall be construed
accordingly, -
(a) ‘Act’ means the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 (50 of 2019);
(b) ‘Applicant’ means –
(i) a body corporate incorporated outside India and authorised by foreign insurer(s) under a
written contract to manage part of its direct insurance business including solicitation,
underwriting risks and/or settling the claims; or
(ii) a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 (No. 18 of 2013);
Explanation. - For removal of doubts, it is clarified that the term ‘body corporate’ under
this clause shall not include Limited Liability Company.
(c) ‘Authority’ means the International Financial Services Centres Authority established under sub-
section (1) of Section 4 of the Act;
(d) ‘Binding Authority Agreement (BAA)’ means a written contract executed between an MGA and a
foreign insurer under which a foreign insurer authorises the MGA to act as an agent and to enter
into a contract of insurance on its behalf; setting forth the terms, conditions for binding insurance
risks or settlement of claims;
(e) ‘Board of the Applicant’ means a ‘Board’ as defined under the Companies Act, 2013 (No. 18 of
2013) or a body discharging equivalent functions, by whatever name called;
(f) ‘Competent Authority’ means:
(i) Chairperson; or
(ii) such Whole-Time Member or such Committee of the Whole-Time Members or Officer (s)
of the Authority, as may be determined by the Chairperson.
(g) ‘Domestic Tariff Area (DTA)’ means the whole of India (including the territorial waters and
continental shelf) but does not include the areas of the Special Economic Zones;
(h) ‘Fiduciary Account’ means a designated account against each foreign insurer, maintained by an
MGA, with an IFSC Banking Unit exclusively for holding premiums or claim settlements, or
both on behalf of such foreign insurer;
(i) ‘Gross Written Premium (GWP)’ means the total amount of premium received by an MGA on
behalf of foreign insurer(s);
(j) ‘Foreign Insurer’ means a body corporate incorporated under the law of any country outside India
and duly registered with its home country regulatory or supervisory authority for transacting
direct insurance business;
(k) ‘International Financial Services Centre (IFSC)’ shall have the same meaning as assigned to it
under clause (g) of sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Act;
(l) ‘IFSC Banking Unit (IBU)’ means a unit licensed by the Authority to undertake permissible
activities under International Financial Services Centres Authority (Banking) Regulations, 2020;
(m) ‘Managing General Agent (MGA)’ means an insurance intermediary registered under these
regulations;
(n) ‘MGA Qualified Person (MQP)’ means an individual who is an employee or director of the MGA
engaged in solicitation, underwriting risks and/or settlement of claims of direct insurance
business, and who has undergone such training and passed such examination as may be specified
by the Competent Authority;
(o) ‘Net Worth’ shall have the same meaning assigned to it in the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013);
(p) ‘Principal Officer’ means a designated employee of the MGA responsible for day-to-day affairs or
conduct of its overall activities, including regulatory compliances of an MGA;
Explanation.- In case of an MGA set up in form of a branch in the IFSC, the expression
‘Principal Officer’ shall be construed as ‘Branch Head’.
(q) ‘Specified Foreign Currency’ means the currencies specified in the First Schedule of the
International Financial Services Centres Authority (Banking) Regulations, 2020, as amended
from time to time; and
(r) ‘Underwriting’ refers to the process of accepting or rejecting insurance risk or insurance liability
by an MGA on behalf of the foreign insurer.
(2) Words and expressions used and not defined in these regulations but defined in the Act or Insurance
Act, 1938 (4 of 1938) or Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999 (41 of 1999) or
Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013) or any rules, regulations made thereunder, shall have the same
meanings respectively assigned to them in those Acts, rules or regulations or any statutory modification
or re-enactment thereto, as the case may be.
CHAPTER II
ELIGIBILITY AND REGISTRATION
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Defines the terms used across the regulations. Note the deliberate carve-outs: an LLC is excluded from 'body corporate' as an applicant, and a branch MGA reads 'Principal Officer' as 'Branch Head'. Undefined terms borrow their meaning from the IFSCA Act, Insurance Act 1938, IRDA Act 1999 or Companies Act 2013.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Two definitions do quiet heavy lifting. 'Applicant' splits the world into a foreign-registered entity setting up a branch and a company freshly incorporated in the IFSC, and the LLP/LLC exclusion closes a structuring route some promoters would otherwise attempt. 'Foreign Insurer' requires home-country registration for direct insurance business — a reinsurer parent alone will not qualify the arrangement.
regulation_content.interview_point: Why does the definition of 'body corporate' expressly exclude an LLC, and what structuring attempt is that exclusion designed to shut down?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Act = 50 of 2019; Insurance Act = 4 of 1938; Companies Act = 18 of 2013

regulation_content.regulation_text:
4. Eligibility criteria
(1) An Applicant registered or licensed to undertake activities akin to an MGA in a jurisdiction outside
India, and desirous of setting up branch in an IFSC shall meet with the following requirements:
(a) It holds a valid certificate of registration or license issued by its home country regulatory or
supervisory authority to undertake activities akin to an MGA;
(b) It has acted as an agent to undertake activities akin to MGA including solicitation, underwriting
risks and/or settling the claims for direct insurance business;
(c) It is registered or certified in a National Regulatory Environment with whom the Government of
India has signed Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement; and
(d) It has obtained ‘No-objection certificate’ from its home country regulatory or supervisory body to
establish a branch in IFSC.
(2) Applicants other than those covered under sub-regulation (1), shall be incorporated under the
Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013) in the IFSC.
(3) An Applicant shall at the time of filing application shall have at least one written contract with a foreign
insurer to manage part of their direct insurance business including an authority to solicit, underwrite
risks and/or settle the claims.
(4) An Applicant having written contract with a foreign insurer to manage part of their direct insurance
business including solicitation, underwriting risks and/or settling the claims shall ensure that such
foreign insurer –
(a) is registered or licensed for transacting direct insurance business, in its home country or country of
its incorporation or domicile;
(b) has satisfactory track record in respect of regulatory or supervisory compliance in its home country
or country of incorporation or domicile and also in any other country in which it is functioning;
(c) has minimum Net Worth of USD 100 Million;
(d) has a minimum credit rating of ‘A’ or its equivalent from any of the internationally renowned credit
rating agencies for the last three years from the date of filing application under these regulations;
(e) is registered or certified in a National Regulatory Environment with whom the Government of India
has signed Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement;
(f) submits Board resolution undertaking to meet all liabilities arising out of Applicant’s operations in
the IFSC;
(g) submits all the details and information as may be required and complies with any additional
requirements as may be specified by the Competent Authority; and
(h) submits undertaking(s) to comply with the provisions of regulation 22 of these regulations.
(5) The Applicant entity, the foreign insurer(s) and their promoters, partners or controlling shareholders
shall be from a jurisdiction which has not been identified in the public statement of Financial Action
Task Force (FATF) as “High-Risk Jurisdiction subject to call for action”.
(6) An Applicant executing or proposing to execute written contract with more than one foreign insurer to
manage part of their direct insurance business including solicitation, underwriting risks and/or settling
the claims shall ensure that above provisions are complied by each such foreign insurer.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the entry conditions for an MGA. A foreign applicant establishing a branch must satisfy home-jurisdiction licensing, relevant MGA experience, DTAA-jurisdiction and NOC requirements. Other applicants must be incorporated under the Companies Act in IFSC. The applicant must also have a written contract with at least one qualifying foreign insurer, and each foreign insurer must satisfy the specified regulatory, net-worth, rating and jurisdiction tests.
regulation_content.practical_point: The foreign-insurer conditions are a material part of the eligibility assessment. In particular, the USD 100 million net-worth and three-year 'A' rating requirements need documentary support.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Create an eligibility file covering applicant form, foreign-insurer licence, track record, net worth, rating history, DTAA jurisdiction, Board undertakings and FATF status.
regulation_content.example: A foreign insurer with USD 120 million net worth and an 'A' rating for the required period still needs to satisfy the remaining conditions.
regulation_content.risk_point: Eligibility is a continuing condition, not a one-time gate — Reg 8(5) requires compliance with Reg 4 'at all times'. Inspections test the live position: the foreign insurer's USD 100 million net worth, its 'A' rating currency, and the DTAA/FATF status. A lapse in any of these after registration is a default trigger under Reg 34.
regulation_content.interview_point: An applicant's foreign insurer partner is rated 'A-' by one agency but 'BBB+' by another, and its net worth is USD 90 million. Which limbs of Reg 4(4) fail, and can the applicant proceed on the strength of the higher rating?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Foreign insurer Net Worth ≥ USD 100 million; credit rating ≥ 'A' for last 3 years; FATF non-high-risk; DTAA jurisdiction
regulation_content.applicability: All MGA applicants and their foreign insurer partners

regulation_content.regulation_text:
5. Procedure for making application
(1) An Applicant desirous of obtaining a certificate of registration from the Authority as an MGA shall
submit an application in such form and be accompanied by such documents as may be specified by the
Competent Authority, along with the applicable fee specified under regulation 29 of these regulations,
on the online platform designated by the Authority.
(2) The Competent Authority may require the Applicant to furnish any additional information or
clarification for considering the Application.
(3) An Applicant after filing of application shall forthwith bring to the notice of the Competent Authority,
on its own, such further information or clarification, which might have a bearing on consideration of its
application.
(4) If the Competent Authority, upon examination of the application, is of the opinion that the registration
cannot be granted, it shall communicate the deficiencies to the Applicant giving it thirty (30) days’ time
to rectify them.
(5) If the Applicant fails to rectify such deficiencies to the satisfaction of the Competent Authority within
the specified time, the Competent Authority may dispose the application and shall communicate the
same to the Applicant, with reasons thereto;
Provided that no such refusal shall be made by the Competent Authority without giving the Applicant
an opportunity to make written submissions on the grounds on which the registration is proposed to be
refused.
(6) Notwithstanding anything contained in these regulations, while granting registration, the Competent
Authority may impose additional conditions to be complied with by an MGA.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the application process, including online filing, supporting documents, additional information requests, a 30-day deficiency rectification window and an opportunity to make written submissions before refusal.
regulation_content.practical_point: Treat the application as a continuing disclosure process; further material information should be brought to the Competent Authority's notice.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Track filing, information requests, deficiency letters and the 30-day response period.
regulation_content.risk_point: The 30-day rectification window runs from the Authority's deficiency notice, and a refusal cannot be issued without a written-submission opportunity first. Missing the window, or treating the deficiency letter as a negotiation rather than a deadline, is the common way applications lapse.
regulation_content.important_numbers: 30 days to rectify deficiencies; fee under Reg 29

regulation_content.provision_heading: Consideration of application for obtaining Certificate of Registration
regulation_content.regulation_text:
6. Consideration of application for obtaining Certificate of Registration–
(1) No person shall act as an MGA without obtaining a certificate of registration from the Competent
Authority under these regulations.
(2) The Competent Authority shall, while examining the application, consider all matters which are
necessary for carrying out the functions of an MGA, including but not limited to the following:
(a) whether the Applicant undertakes to fulfil the capital and Net Worth requirements as specified in
regulation 13 of these regulations to the satisfaction of the Competent Authority;
(b) whether the Applicant has the requisite underwriting and/or claims processing competence and
personnel having necessary qualification and experience, as may be specified by the Competent
Authority;
(c) whether the Principal Officer, promoters, directors, and KMPs/controlling shareholders are ‘Fit and
Proper persons’ as per the criteria specified by the Competent Authority;
(d) whether the Applicant has proposed to appoint a Principal Officer who shall be in direct
employment of the MGA and resident in India;
(e) whether the Applicant has adequate office space, IT systems, and data security protocols within the
IFSC to effectively discharge its activities, that is commensurate with the proposed operations; and
(f) whether the issue of certificate of registration to the Applicant will be in the interest of
policyholders.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the matters considered before registration, including capital/net worth, underwriting or claims competence, fit-and-proper status, Principal Officer, IFSC office/IT/data-security capability and policyholder interest.
regulation_content.practical_point: Registration is not only a financial-capacity test; operational capability and key-person suitability are expressly relevant.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain evidence of personnel competence, fit-and-proper checks, Principal Officer appointment, premises, IT systems and data-security arrangements.
regulation_content.risk_point: The 'fit and proper' assessment reaches promoters, directors, KMPs and controlling shareholders, not just the Principal Officer. A single controlling shareholder with an adverse regulatory history can sink the application even where the operating team is clean.
regulation_content.interview_point: The Authority is examining an application under Reg 6(2). Name the six matters it must be satisfied on, and identify which one goes to the individuals behind the MGA rather than the entity.
regulation_content.important_numbers: PO must be in direct employment of the MGA and resident in India

regulation_content.provision_heading: Procedure for issuance of Certificate of Registration
regulation_content.regulation_text:
7. Procedure for issuance of Certificate of Registration
(1) On consideration of the application, the Competent Authority may grant in-principle approval to the
applicant, subject to satisfaction that the Applicant has fulfilled the conditions as specified under sub-
regulation (2) of regulation 6 of these regulations and upon payment of applicable fees.
(2) The Competent Authority on being satisfied with the compliance under sub-regulation (1) and also with
other compliances under these regulations, including capital requirement, Net Worth requirement and
professional indemnity policy, may issue a certificate of registration.
(3) Registration granted under these regulations shall remain in force subject to conditions as specified
under these regulations, until such registration is suspended or cancelled by the Competent Authority.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the two-stage grant: in-principle approval once the Reg 6(2) conditions and fees are met, then the certificate of registration once capital, net worth and the professional indemnity policy are all in place. Registration then continues until suspended or cancelled.
regulation_content.practical_point: In-principle approval should not be treated as permission to commence MGA activity.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Keep the in-principle approval, fee evidence and final certificate together with all conditions.
regulation_content.important_numbers: In-principle → final CoR; PI policy required before issuance

regulation_content.provision_heading: Conditions upon issuance of Certificate of Registration
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Lists the standing conditions attached to registration — sixteen in all. The MGA must trade only the registered business in the Schedule-I manner, keep a live BAA and Letter of Approval, stay within eligibility at all times, follow the AML/CFT/KYC guidelines and the grievance-redressal circular, never do multi-level marketing, and keep its shares unencumbered.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: These conditions convert one-time entry criteria into perpetual obligations — the phrase 'at all times' recurs deliberately. Condition (2) pulling in Section 42D(5) of the Insurance Act, and condition (7) requiring a subsisting SEZ Letter of Approval, are the two most often overlooked because they sit outside the MGA regulations themselves.
regulation_content.practical_point: This is the central post-registration conditions provision and should be converted into an internal conditions register.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain a condition-of-registration checklist and test each condition periodically.
regulation_content.risk_point: Each of the sixteen conditions is independently enforceable; breach of any one is a Reg 34 default ground. Inspection tends to probe the unencumbered-shares condition (15) and the live-BAA condition (4), because both are easy to let slip after onboarding.
regulation_content.interview_point: An MGA pledges its promoter's shares to secure a working-capital line six months after registration. Which registration condition does this breach, and what is the consequence under Reg 34?
regulation_content.important_numbers: 16 standing conditions; MLM prohibited; shares unencumbered at all times

regulation_content.regulation_text:
9. Commencement of business-
(1) An MGA shall commence business within a period of one hundred eighty (180) days from the date of
grant of certificate of registration by the Competent Authority;
Provided that, if an MGA fails to commence business within the said period, it can, before the
expiration and at least thirty (30) days prior to such expiry, make an application to the Competent
Authority seeking extension of time.
(2) Upon receipt of an application under sub-regulation (1), the Competent Authority may examine the
same and communicate the decision there on, in writing to such applicant;
Provided that no extension of time shall be granted by the Competent Authority beyond eighteen (18)
months from the date of grant of certificate of registration.
CHAPTER III
REQUIREMENTS FOR AN MGA
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The MGA must start business within 180 days of the certificate date. If it cannot, it must apply for extension before expiry and at least 30 days ahead; the Authority can extend, but never beyond 18 months from the certificate date.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The two clocks are easy to conflate. The 180 days is the commencement deadline; the 18 months is the absolute outer limit on any extension — not a fresh grant. An MGA that drifts past 180 days without a timely extension application has no cure, because the proviso requires the application to precede expiry.
regulation_content.practical_point: The commencement clock runs from the certificate date.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Record the certificate date, 180-day deadline and any extension approval.
regulation_content.example: If registration is granted on 1 July, plan commencement well before the 180-day deadline and seek extension in time if required.
regulation_content.risk_point: Failure to commence within 180 days (or the granted extension) is an express cancellation ground under Reg 34(1)(q). The diarising failure — applying for extension after the 180 days has run — is fatal and cannot be argued around.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Commence within 180 days; extension application ≥ 30 days before expiry; outer limit 18 months from CoR date

regulation_content.regulation_text:
10. Scope of Operations –
(1) An MGA is permitted to undertake the activities of direct insurance business in the IFSC, outside India,
or both.
(2) An MGA shall not solicit direct insurance business from the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) in India,
except in accordance with Section 2CB of the Insurance Act, 1938 (4 of 1938).
(3) An MGA shall undertake direct insurance business, in accordance with the provisions of these
regulations, including any terms and conditions stipulated under the certificate of registration.
(4) An MGA shall carry out its operation in any of the Specified Foreign Currencies;
Provided that, an MGA may open an INR account to defray its administrative and statutory expenses
and for such other purposes as may be permitted under the applicable laws.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Fixes the operating perimeter: an MGA may write direct insurance business in the IFSC, outside India, or both, but cannot solicit from the Domestic Tariff Area except as Section 2CB of the Insurance Act allows. Business is done in a Specified Foreign Currency; an INR account is permitted only for administrative and statutory expenses.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The DTA carve-out is the line most likely to be tested. An MGA sitting in GIFT City is geographically close to the Indian mainland market but regulatorily walled off from it — soliciting a domestic policyholder without the Section 2CB gateway is a perimeter breach, not a mere technicality.
regulation_content.practical_point: The geographic permission does not override the statutory restriction on DTA solicitation.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Map target markets and solicitation channels before launch.
regulation_content.risk_point: DTA solicitation is where an MGA most easily strays. Marketing that reaches Indian mainland prospects — including via digital channels under Reg 28 — must be tested against the Section 2CB exception before it goes out.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Currency: Specified Foreign Currency; INR account only for admin/statutory expenses

regulation_content.simple_explanation: Four hard prohibitions: no binding reinsurance or retrocession for the foreign insurer, no participation in insurance/reinsurance syndicates, no assignment or sub-delegation of underwriting or claims authority, and no joint employment of a person already employed by the foreign insurer.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Prohibition (3) is the structural spine of the whole framework — delegated authority cannot be re-delegated. An MGA that outsources underwriting or claims decisioning to a third-party administrator, however competent, has assigned authority it was never permitted to pass on.
regulation_content.practical_point: Delegated authority remains bounded; the MGA cannot pass it onward.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Include the prohibitions in the operating policy and BAA control checklist.
regulation_content.risk_point: Sub-delegation is the subtle trap: engaging a TPA for claims or an external underwriting agency looks operationally sensible but breaches prohibition (3). Inspection will follow the decision trail to see who actually exercised the delegated authority.
regulation_content.interview_point: An MGA appoints a specialist third-party underwriting agency to price a complex marine risk on its behalf. Is this permitted? Identify the specific prohibition engaged.
regulation_content.important_numbers: 4 prohibited activities

regulation_content.provision_heading: Executing BAA with other foreign insurer(s)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
12. Executing BAA with other foreign insurer(s) – An MGA executing BAA with another foreign insurer(s),
shall mutatis mutandis comply with provisions of sub-regulations (3), (4) and (5) of regulation 4 and regulation
20 of these regulations.
Explanation. - An MGA shall, at all times, maintain above-referred documents and shall submit the same as
and when sought by the Competent Authority.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Where an MGA signs a BAA with an additional foreign insurer, the eligibility limbs in Reg 4(3),(4),(5) and the BAA requirements in Reg 20 apply again, mutatis mutandis, to that new relationship. The supporting documents must be kept ready for the Authority on demand.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This closes the multi-principal loophole: each foreign insurer relationship is vetted on its own eligibility footing. An MGA cannot use one qualifying insurer as a passport to bind risks for a second insurer that would not itself clear Reg 4.
regulation_content.practical_point: Each foreign-insurer relationship should be assessed separately.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain a separate eligibility and BAA file for each foreign insurer.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Re-applies Reg 4(3),(4),(5) and Reg 20 per additional insurer

regulation_content.regulation_text:
13. Capital and Net Worth Requirements
(1) An MGA, set up in the form of a company, shall maintain a minimum paid-up equity capital equivalent
to USD 5,00, 000 (USD Five Lakh only) with an IBU.
(2) An MGA, set up in the form of a branch, shall maintain a minimum assigned capital equivalent to USD
5,00, 000 (USD Five Lakh only) with an IBU.
(3) An MGA shall maintain Net Worth of minimum equivalent to USD 250,000 (USD Two Lakh Fifty
Thousand only) or 50% of the minimum paid-up or assigned capital, whichever is higher, at all times.
Explanation. - For avoidance of doubts, it is clarified that an MGA set up in form of a branch shall
maintain Net Worth at its parent level.
(4) In case of any shortfall in Net Worth as required under sub-regulation (3) above, the MGA shall
immediately restore the same and report compliance of the same within a period of fifteen (15) days to
the Competent Authority.
(5) The investment made by the promoters/ shareholders in an MGA shall be from their owned funds and
not from any other sources;
Explanation. - For the purpose of this sub-regulation, owned funds shall not include funds arranged by
way of borrowings or loans.
(6) An MGA shall submit a paid-up capital and Net Worth certificate issued by its statutory auditor or an
independent Company Secretary on annual basis, to the Competent Authority.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Prescribes USD 500,000 minimum paid-up equity capital for a company-form MGA or minimum assigned capital for a branch. Net worth must be at least USD 250,000 or 50% of the applicable minimum capital, whichever is higher, at all times. A shortfall must be restored immediately and reported within 15 days.
regulation_content.practical_point: For a company-form MGA, 50% of USD 500,000 is USD 250,000. Branch net worth is maintained at parent level.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Monitor capital and net worth continuously and obtain the annual statutory auditor/independent Company Secretary certificate.
regulation_content.example: A company-form MGA with USD 500,000 paid-up capital must maintain at least USD 250,000 net worth, subject to the 'whichever is higher' test.
regulation_content.risk_point: Two live figures that inspection reconciles to the IBU statements: minimum capital of USD 500,000 and net worth of the higher of USD 250,000 or 50% of capital, 'at all times'. A branch maintains net worth at parent level — a point commonly mis-stated in filings. A shortfall must be restored immediately and reported within 15 days; the 15 days is a reporting deadline, not a cure period.
regulation_content.interview_point: A company-form MGA holds USD 500,000 paid-up capital. Its net worth dips to USD 240,000. Is it compliant? State the test and the reporting obligation, with timing.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Capital USD 500,000 (company: paid-up equity / branch: assigned); Net Worth higher of USD 250,000 or 50% of capital; shortfall restore immediately, report within 15 days; annual capital & net-worth certificate
regulation_content.responsible_person: Statutory Auditor / independent Company Secretary; PO to file

regulation_content.regulation_text:
14. Professional Indemnity - An MGA shall purchase and maintain, at all times, a professional indemnity
insurance cover throughout the validity of its registration in accordance with the Schedule-III of these
regulations;
Provided that an MGA in branch form shall maintain the professional indemnity insurance policy at its head
office and shall have endorsement on such insurance policy to the effect that liabilities if any, arising out of
operations at the IFSC branch office are also covered in such policy.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The MGA must buy and keep professional indemnity cover for the whole registration period, on the terms in Schedule-III. A branch MGA keeps the policy at head office but must endorse it to cover liabilities arising from the IFSC branch's operations.
regulation_content.practical_point: PI cover is a continuing registration condition, not a one-time document.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Track policy expiry, renewal, limits and Schedule III compliance.
regulation_content.risk_point: The branch-endorsement point is the recurring gap: a head-office master PI policy that does not name or extend to the IFSC branch's acts leaves the branch effectively uninsured for regulatory purposes.
regulation_content.important_numbers: PI cover throughout registration; Schedule-III terms; branch endorsement mandatory

regulation_content.regulation_text:
15. Financial security and Deposit requirements
(1) An MGA shall, before the commencement of their business, deposit and keep deposited with any IBU,
with lien marked in favour of the Authority, a sum equivalent to –
(a) USD 10,000 (USD Ten thousand only), which shall not be released without the prior written
permission of the Competent Authority; and
(b) 10% of the minimum paid-up equity capital or assigned capital as specified under regulation 13 of
these regulations, which shall not be released without the prior written permission of the
Competent Authority;
Provided that the Competent Authority may impose a separate limit of deposit, in any case not
exceeding USD 1,00,000 (USD One Lakh only).
Explanation. - For removal of doubts, it is clarified that the interest earned on such deposit shall not be
subject to lien with the Authority.
(2) An MGA shall furnish to the Competent Authority, as and when called upon to do so, a non-
encumbrance statement from the IBU with which such deposit is maintained.
(3) The Competent Authority may appropriate such amount from the deposit maintained in accordance with
sub-regulation (1), as required to settle unpaid ‘Courts/Ombudsman Awards’ or ‘Claims under
adjudication’ in case liquidation proceedings are initiated against the concerned MGA.
CHAPTER IV
OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Before commencing business the MGA lodges a lien-marked deposit with an IBU equal to USD 10,000 plus 10% of the minimum paid-up/assigned capital; the Authority may instead set a single cap not exceeding USD 1,00,000. Interest on the deposit is outside the lien. The Authority can appropriate the deposit to meet Court/Ombudsman awards or claims under adjudication if the MGA goes into liquidation.
regulation_content.practical_point: The deposit has a regulatory protection function and may be appropriated in specified liquidation situations.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain the deposit and obtain the non-encumbrance statement when required.
regulation_content.example: For USD 500,000 minimum capital, the 10% component is USD 50,000, in addition to USD 10,000, subject to the Competent Authority's separate limit.
regulation_content.risk_point: The deposit protects policyholders on liquidation, so a non-encumbrance statement from the IBU must be producible on demand. Releasing or re-hypothecating the deposit without prior written permission is a serious default.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Deposit = USD 10,000 + 10% of min capital; Authority cap ≤ USD 100,000; interest outside lien

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.regulation_text:
16. Ownership and control of shares- Any change(s) in the beneficial ownership of shares or contribution and
control of the MGA shall be made only with prior approval of the Competent Authority and in such manner
and process as may be specified by the Competent Authority.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Any change in beneficial ownership, contribution or control of the MGA needs the Authority's prior approval, in the manner it specifies.
regulation_content.practical_point: Ownership changes should be treated as regulatory events, not merely corporate actions.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Build a prior-approval trigger into the share-transfer and corporate-action process.
regulation_content.risk_point: 'Beneficial' ownership is the operative word — an upstream change at the parent that shifts ultimate control triggers the approval even where the immediate IFSC shareholding is untouched.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Prior approval for any change in ownership/control

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.regulation_text:
17. Board approved policy
(1) An MGA shall have a Board approved policy containing the manner of soliciting, underwriting risks,
settlement of claims of direct insurance business and acceptance of risk servicing insurance policies
including suitability requirements.
(2) The Board approved policy shall, inter-alia, include the approach to be followed by an MGA in having
multiple tie-ups, type of products sold, mode of solicitation, grievance redressal mechanism, reporting
requirements and any other requirement with regard to different business segments.
(3) The Board approved policy shall be reviewed at least once in every three (3) years by its Board by
whatever name called.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The MGA needs a Board-approved policy covering how it solicits, underwrites, settles claims and accepts risk-servicing policies, including suitability. The policy must address multiple tie-ups, product types, solicitation mode, grievance redressal and reporting, and be reviewed by the Board at least once every three years.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Note the asymmetry: the conflict-management policy under Reg 24(4) is reviewed annually, but this operating policy is a three-year cycle. Practitioners frequently apply the wrong review frequency to the wrong policy.
regulation_content.practical_point: The policy should translate the Regulations and each BAA into operating rules for each business segment.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain Board approval, version control and the three-year review record.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Board policy; reviewed ≥ once every 3 years

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.regulation_text:
18. Code of conduct - An MGA shall perform its functions and duties, and exercise its delegated authority, in
strict adherence to the Code of Conduct and operational standards specified in Schedule-II of these regulations.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The MGA must perform its functions and exercise delegated authority in strict adherence to the Code of Conduct and operational standards in Schedule-II.
regulation_content.practical_point: Treat the Code as an operating standard rather than a standalone document.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Map Schedule II requirements to underwriting, claims, marketing, conflicts and records controls.

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.regulation_text:
19. Internal control and systems - An MGA shall develop and maintain a suitable internal control system,
including an audit system, commensurate with the size, nature, scale and complexity of its business operations.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Requires an internal control system, including an audit system, proportionate to the size, nature, scale and complexity of the MGA's business.
regulation_content.practical_point: The control environment should grow with delegated authority and transaction volume.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Document key controls, owners, testing frequency and internal audit coverage.

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.regulation_text:
20. Binding Authority Agreement (BAA)
(1) An MGA shall not solicit business, underwrite risks or settle claims on behalf of a foreign insurer,
unless a BAA containing the clauses as specified under Schedule-IV of these regulations is executed
with the concerned foreign insurer and submitted to the Competent Authority.
(2) The BAA shall, inter-alia, explicitly include the following: -
(a) classes of direct insurance business, territorial limits and maximum limits of liability per risk;
(b) underwriting guidelines and the basis of rates to be charged;
(c) underwriting capacity allocated by the foreign insurer to an MGA; and
(d) foreign insurer’s right to terminate or suspend the BAA, including the details of the person
authorized to terminate or suspend the BAA during the pendency of dispute, if any and the ground
of termination or suspension of BAA.
(3) The BAA shall strictly delineate ‘Claims Processing’ and ‘Claims Settlement’ as separate activities that
may be undertaken by an MGA.
(4) Where the authority to settle claims has been granted, an MGA shall settle claims in accordance with the
monetary limit per claim and an aggregate limit as specified in the BAA;
Provided that any claim exceeding USD 10,000 (USD Ten Thousand only) or involving a coverage
dispute shall be referred to the concerned foreign insurer for prior approval.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Requires a Schedule IV-compliant BAA before solicitation, underwriting or claims settlement. The BAA must define business classes, territory, liability limits, underwriting guidelines, capacity and termination/suspension rights. Claims processing and settlement must be separately delineated; claims above USD 10,000 or involving a coverage dispute require foreign-insurer prior approval.
regulation_content.practical_point: The BAA is the operational boundary document for delegated authority. Its authority limits should be testable at transaction level.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Do not permit activity outside the authority matrix in the executed BAA.
regulation_content.example: A claim of USD 12,000, or any claim involving a coverage dispute, must be referred to the foreign insurer for prior approval.
regulation_content.risk_point: The BAA is the licence to operate: no soliciting, underwriting or claims settlement until a Schedule-IV-compliant BAA is executed and filed with the Authority. Inspection reads the BAA for the mandatory clauses and, critically, for the claims-authority limits — any single claim above USD 10,000 or involving a coverage dispute must go back to the insurer for prior approval.
regulation_content.interview_point: An MGA holds settlement authority up to USD 25,000 per claim in its BAA. A claim comes in at USD 12,000 with no coverage dispute. Can the MGA settle it? Reconcile the BAA limit with the Reg 20(4) proviso.
regulation_content.important_numbers: BAA must precede business; Schedule-IV clauses; claims > USD 10,000 or coverage-dispute → insurer prior approval

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.regulation_text:
21. Fiduciary Accounts and premium segregation
(1) Where an MGA is permitted to collect the premium and remit the same to the foreign insurer and/or
collect the claims due from the foreign insurer in order to pass on to the policyholder(s), the money thus
collected shall be maintained in a Fiduciary Account.
(2) The money collected by an MGA in the Fiduciary Account shall be segregated from other accounts
maintained by such MGA.
(3) The money collected by an MGA in the Fiduciary Account shall only be used for the permitted purposes
and shall not be used for any other purposes.
(4) An MGA shall not retain more than three (03) months' worth of losses and loss adjustment expenses in
the Fiduciary Account, and any such surplus amount shall be remitted to the foreign insurer, monthly.
(5) The money held in the Fiduciary Account, being the money of policyholders or of the foreign insurer, as
the case may be, shall not be liable to attachment or be part of the assets of the MGA in the event of its
insolvency or liquidation.
(6) The Fiduciary Account shall only be used for the following purposes–
(a) Credits: Receipt of premiums from policyholders; receipt of claim funds/return premiums from
foreign insurers; and interest earned on such funds (subject to the BAA);
(b) Debits: Remittance of premiums to foreign insurers; payment of claims/refunds to policyholders;
and withdrawal of commission as per the BAA.
(7) An MGA shall submit a certificate issued by its statutory auditor to the Competent Authority on half
yearly basis confirming compliance with fund segregation requirements specified under these
regulations.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Creates the fiduciary-account framework for premiums and claim funds, requiring segregation, restricted use, a three-month loss/loss-adjustment-expense ceiling, monthly remittance of surplus and half-yearly auditor certification.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The account is 'against each foreign insurer' — per the definition in Reg 3(h) — so an MGA with several principals runs several fiduciary accounts, not one pooled account. Commingling across insurers defeats the segregation the section is built to guarantee.
regulation_content.practical_point: The fiduciary account is not ordinary MGA working capital; it holds policyholder/foreign-insurer money for restricted purposes.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Reconcile the account, document permitted credits/debits and obtain the half-yearly auditor certificate.
regulation_content.risk_point: The fiduciary account is ring-fenced policyholder/insurer money — not the MGA's asset, and immune from attachment on the MGA's insolvency. The two controls inspection tests are the strict credits/debits list and the three-month cap on retained losses and loss-adjustment expenses, with any surplus swept to the insurer monthly. A statutory-auditor certificate confirming segregation goes to the Authority half-yearly.
regulation_content.interview_point: An MGA keeps four months of loss funds in the fiduciary account to smooth claims payments. Is this permissible, and what must happen to the surplus month?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Retain ≤ 3 months' losses & LAE; sweep surplus monthly; segregation certificate half-yearly

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.provision_heading: Duties of foreign insurer(s) and their operational oversight
regulation_content.regulation_text:
22. Duties of foreign insurer(s) and their operational oversight-
(1) The foreign insurer who has executed the BAA with an MGA shall –
(a) conduct an independent annual audit of the records of the MGA to satisfy that the MGA complies
with the BAA and the Net Worth requirements as specified under these regulations; and
(b) conduct an on-site review of the MGA’s underwriting and claims processing at least on a half yearly
basis.
(2) If an MGA establishes loss reserves, the relevant foreign insurer shall annually obtain the opinion of an
independent actuary certifying their adequacy.
Explanation. - For removal of doubts, it is clarified that the above requirement shall be in addition to
any other required loss reserve certification.
(3) The foreign insurer shall not –
(a) appoint any officer, director, employee or controlling shareholder of the MGA on its Board; and
(b) give binding authority to an MGA of more than ten per cent (10%) of its GWP for the previous
financial year.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Puts oversight duties on the foreign insurer, not the MGA: an independent annual audit of the MGA's records, a half-yearly on-site review of underwriting and claims, an annual independent actuarial opinion where the MGA holds loss reserves, a bar on appointing MGA personnel to the insurer's Board, and a 10%-of-GWP ceiling on binding authority given to any one MGA.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This is the one substantive section that binds the foreign insurer through the MGA framework — which is why the Reg 4(4)(h) undertaking to comply with Reg 22 is taken from the insurer up front. The 10% GWP binding-authority cap is a concentration control: no single MGA may hold delegated authority for more than a tenth of the insurer's prior-year GWP.
regulation_content.practical_point: The model keeps the foreign insurer actively responsible for oversight of delegated authority.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Coordinate the annual audit and half-yearly on-site review calendar with each foreign insurer.
regulation_content.example: If prior-year GWP is USD 50 million, the 10% binding-authority ceiling is USD 5 million.
regulation_content.interview_point: Why does the MGA framework impose duties directly on the foreign insurer under Reg 22, and how is that obligation secured at the application stage?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Independent audit annual; on-site review half-yearly; actuarial opinion annual (if reserves); binding authority ≤ 10% of prior-year GWP

regulation_content.chapter_title: OPERATIONS, CODE OF CONDUCT AND MANAGEMENT
regulation_content.provision_heading: Maintenance of books of accounts and records
regulation_content.regulation_text:
23. Maintenance of books of accounts and records-
(1) An MGA set up in the form of a company shall prepare and maintain the following financial
statements–
(a) a balance sheet as at the end of each financial year;
(b) a profit and loss account for that period, which shall be maintained on accrual basis;
(c) a statement of cash/fund flow (direct method) for that period; and
(d) additional statements on its business as may be specified by the Competent Authority.
Explanation. -
(i) For the purposes of this regulation, the financial year for an MGA in form of a branch in the IFSC
shall refer to the financial year as specified by its home country’s regulatory or supervisory
authority;
(ii) the financial year for an MGA set up in the form of a company shall refer to a period of twelve (12)
months commencing from 1st April and ending on the 31st March.
(2) An MGA in branch form shall prepare and maintain the financial statements in accordance with the
accounting standards as specified by its home country regulatory or supervisory authority.
(3) An MGA shall submit to the Competent Authority the audited financial statements within a period of
thirty (30) days of the annual general meeting on or before 30th September every year, whichever is
earlier, along with director’s report, as applicable, the remarks or observations of the auditor, if any, on
the conduct of the business, state of accounts, etc.
(5) An MGA shall take steps to rectify the deficiencies, if any, made out in the auditor’s report, and inform
the Competent Authority about the same within a period of ninety (90) days from the date of the
auditor’s report.
(6) All the financial statements and relevant documents shall be maintained at the office of the MGA in the
IFSC and shall be available for inspection by the Competent Authority.
(7) All claim files shall be the joint property of the foreign insurer and the MGA;
Provided that upon an order of liquidation of the foreign insurer, all such files shall become the sole
property of the foreign insurer or its estate, subject to the condition that the MGA shall have access to
and the right to copy the files on a timely basis.
(8) An MGA shall render accounts, including claims bordereaux, to the foreign insurer stating details of all
transactions and remit all funds due under the contract to the foreign insurer on not less than a monthly
basis.
(9) All financial statements and relevant documents referred to in these regulations shall be retained for
such period as specified under the International Financial Services Centres Authority (Maintenance of
Insurance Records and Submission of Requisite Information for Investigation and Inspection)
Regulations, 2022;
Provided that the documents pertaining to the cases where claims are reported and the decision is
pending in a Court, the documents shall be maintained till the disposal of the cases;
Provided further that unless otherwise required in any other laws for the time being in force, all such
financial statements and relevant documents may be maintained in non-editable electronic retrieval
form.
(10) All financial statements shall include a note providing the foreign insurer-wise (including foreign
insurer’s group companies) details of all the incomes received by it and also the details of payments
received by it from its group companies, associates, and related parties.
(11) An MGA shall make disclosures of all related party transactions in its audited financial statements.
(12) An MGA shall have robust cyber security and cyber resilience framework in accordance with the
requirements as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.
CHAPTER V
GOVERNANCE AND COMPLIANCE
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the books-and-records regime. A company-form MGA prepares a balance sheet, accrual-basis P&L and direct-method cash-flow each financial year (1 April–31 March); a branch follows its home regulator's accounting standards and financial year. Audited financials go to the Authority within 30 days of the AGM or by 30 September, whichever is earlier; auditor-flagged deficiencies are cured and reported within 90 days. Claim files are joint MGA/insurer property, related-party transactions are disclosed, and a robust cyber-security framework is maintained.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Note the drafting gap in the source — sub-regulation (4) is absent between (3) and (5). This is a numbering artefact in the gazette, not a missing obligation; the substance runs (1),(2),(3),(5),(6)… The record-retention period is pinned to the IFSCA (Maintenance of Insurance Records) Regulations, 2022, with pending-litigation files kept until disposal.
regulation_content.practical_point: This provision connects statutory accounts with operational records and cyber controls.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain the IFSC records repository, audit calendar, related-party register and cyber-resilience evidence.
regulation_content.risk_point: Two timing traps: the '30 days of AGM or 30 September, whichever earlier' filing (the earlier of the two governs, not the later), and the 90-day auditor-deficiency cure clock that runs from the auditor's report date, not the filing date.
regulation_content.important_numbers: FY 1 Apr–31 Mar (company); audited financials within 30 days of AGM or by 30 Sep, whichever earlier; rectify auditor deficiencies within 90 days; monthly remittance/accounts to insurer

regulation_content.regulation_text:
24. Foundational Principles for an MGA- An MGA shall, at all times, act in accordance with the following
foundational principles -
(1) An MGA owes its primary fiduciary duty to the foreign insurer with whom it has executed a BAA and
while exercising delegated authority the MGA shall observe high standards of integrity and act with the
such skill and care as if the MGA’s own capital were at risk.
(2) An MGA shall ensure that the interests of policyholders are protected, particularly when exercising
delegated authority for underwriting or claims.
(3) An MGA may use the advertising material approved by the foreign insurer for solicitation of insurance
business.
(4) An MGA shall develop and implement a Board approved conflict management policy, which shall be
reviewed annually.
(5) An MGA shall disclose its status as an insurance intermediary of the foreign insurer(s) to the
policyholders and shall prominently mention the name of the foreign insurer(s) in all policy documents.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: States the foundational principles: the MGA's primary fiduciary duty is to the foreign insurer, exercised with the care it would apply to its own capital at risk, while protecting policyholders' interests; it may use insurer-approved advertising, must run a Board-approved conflict-management policy reviewed annually, and must disclose its intermediary status and name the foreign insurer on all policy documents.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 'primary duty to the insurer, secondary duty to the policyholder' hierarchy is the philosophical core of the MGA model and is easy to state backwards. The MGA is the insurer's agent — not the policyholder's broker — and every conflict rule flows from that ordering.
regulation_content.practical_point: These principles form the conduct baseline for delegated underwriting and claims activity.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Use them as a governance test when reviewing conflicts, marketing and delegated decisions.
regulation_content.interview_point: An MGA faces a pricing decision that favours the policyholder at the foreign insurer's expense. Whose interest ranks first under Reg 24, and how does the secondary duty still constrain the MGA?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Conflict-management policy reviewed annually

regulation_content.regulation_text:
25. Filing of returns - An MGA shall file the relevant returns in such form and manner as may be specified by the
Competent Authority.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The MGA files the relevant returns in the form and manner the Authority specifies.
regulation_content.practical_point: The obligation continues even where detailed formats are specified separately.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain a regulatory returns calendar and evidence of submission.

regulation_content.regulation_text:
26. Disclosures to the Competent Authority -
(1) An MGA shall take prior approval of the Competent Authority for the following –
(a) Change of Principal Officer/ Branch Head;
(b) Change of Director(s) if any;
(c) Change of its name; or
(d) Change of its corporate/registered office.
Explanation. – For removal of doubts, it is clarified that an MGA shall inform Competent Authority in
the event of resignation of any director.
(2) An MGA, within seven (07) days, shall furnish to the Competent Authority the following information as
and when there is a change in the information furnished previously to the Competent Authority:
(a) List of MQPs; and
(b) Claims under the Professional Indemnity Policy.
(3) The Competent Authority may require the MGA to furnish such other data, documents or information,
in such manner and at such interval, as it may specify.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Splits notifications into prior-approval and post-event categories. Prior approval is needed to change the Principal Officer/Branch Head, directors, name or registered office; a director's resignation must be intimated. Separately, within 7 days of any change the MGA furnishes the updated MQP list and any claims made under the PI policy.
regulation_content.practical_point: Separate prior-approval events from seven-day change reporting.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Create an approval/intimation matrix covering each event and owner.
regulation_content.risk_point: The distinction is what gets missed: PO and director changes are prior-approval items, but the MQP list and PI-claim updates are 7-day post-event filings. Treating a PO change as a mere intimation, or the MQP update as needing approval, both misread the section.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Prior approval: PO/director/name/office change; 7 days: MQP list & PI claims

regulation_content.regulation_text:
27. Amalgamation and transfer of business
(1) No scheme of amalgamation or merger or acquisition or transfer of business of the MGA shall be
implemented without the prior approval of the Competent Authority.
(2) The process for seeking approval, for such amalgamation or merger or acquisition or transfer of
business of the MGA, shall be in such form and manner as specified by the Competent Authority.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: No amalgamation, merger, acquisition or transfer of the MGA's business may be implemented without the Authority's prior approval, in the form and manner it specifies.
regulation_content.practical_point: Corporate restructuring cannot be treated as a purely Companies Act transaction where the MGA business is affected.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Obtain regulatory approval before implementation and retain it with transaction documents.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Prior approval for M&A / transfer

regulation_content.provision_heading: Sale of insurance through digital modes
regulation_content.regulation_text:
28. Sale of insurance through digital modes
(1) An MGA may enter into an agreement with foreign insurers for sale of insurance products online by
linking to the web portals of the foreign insurers or by establishing insurance self-network platform.
(2) An MGA may solicit insurance through digital modes subject to such conditions as may be specified by
the Competent Authority.
(3) The procedure for sale of insurance products where leads are generated through online or off-line and
completed through tele-marketing mode by MGA shall be as specified by the Competent Authority.
CHAPTER VI
MISCELLANEOUS
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Permits digital distribution: the MGA may contract with foreign insurers to sell online by linking to the insurer's web portal or running its own insurance self-network platform, may solicit through digital modes on the Authority's conditions, and may sell via tele-marketing on generated leads as specified.
regulation_content.practical_point: Digital distribution is permitted subject to the regulatory conditions applicable to the channel.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Review the digital customer journey against the applicable IFSCA conditions before launch.
regulation_content.risk_point: Digital reach makes the Reg 10(2) DTA boundary harder to police — an online journey that a domestic prospect can complete may amount to DTA solicitation. Geo-controls and eligibility screening on the digital funnel are the practical safeguard.

regulation_content.regulation_text:
29. Fee -
(1) The Applicant while filing application seeking registration as an MGA shall pay non-refundable fee of
USD 1,000 (USD One thousand only) as application fees, to the Authority.
(2) Upon communication the Applicant shall pay non-refundable fee of USD 5,000 (USD Five thousand
only) as registration fees, to the Authority.
(3) An MGA who has been granted certificate of registration under these regulations shall pay higher of the
annual fee as specified below, for each financial year to the Authority on or before 30th day of April of
such financial year:
(a) USD 12,500 (USD twelve thousand five hundred only); or
(b) One-twentieth of one per cent. of total gross premium written by an MGA during the financial
year immediately preceding the year in which the annual fee is required to be paid.
(4) The fee amount shall be remitted into the bank account of the Authority through any of the recognised
modes of electronic funds transfer.
(5) In the event of a certificate of registration being lost or destroyed or mutilated, an MGA shall submit an
application along with a fee of USD 500 (USD five hundred only) requesting for the issue of a duplicate
certificate of registration, with a declaration giving full details about the certificate of registration.
(6) The Competent Authority, after satisfying itself that the original certificate of registration has been lost,
destroyed or mutilated, may issue a duplicate certificate of registration with an endorsement thereon that
it is a duplicate.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the fee schedule: USD 1,000 non-refundable application fee, USD 5,000 registration fee on communication, and an annual fee — the higher of USD 12,500 or one-twentieth of one per cent of the year's gross written premium — payable by 30 April each financial year. A lost/mutilated certificate is replaced for USD 500.
regulation_content.practical_point: The annual fee is both turnover-linked and subject to a fixed minimum.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Calculate annual fee from prior-year GWP and complete payment by 30 April.
regulation_content.example: If prior-year GWP is USD 20 million, 0.05% is USD 10,000, so the USD 12,500 minimum applies.
regulation_content.risk_point: The annual fee is a 'higher of' test, not a flat USD 12,500 — a high-GWP MGA underpays if it defaults to the fixed figure. One-twentieth of one per cent is 0.05% of GWP; miscomputing it as 0.5% or 1% is the common arithmetic error.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Application USD 1,000; registration USD 5,000; annual = higher of USD 12,500 or 0.05% of GWP, by 30 Apr; duplicate certificate USD 500

regulation_content.regulation_text:
30. Voluntary surrender- An MGA may surrender its certificate of registration only with the prior written
approval of the Competent Authority and after providing a plan to run off its existing book of business,
including submitting evidence of adequate capital to wind down operations in an orderly manner without
disrupting policyholder services.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An MGA may surrender its registration only with the Authority's prior written approval, after submitting a run-off plan for its existing book with evidence of adequate capital to wind down in an orderly way without disrupting policyholder service.
regulation_content.practical_point: Surrender is an orderly exit process, not simply cancellation of a certificate.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Prepare run-off, capital, policyholder-servicing and foreign-insurer arrangements before seeking surrender.
regulation_content.risk_point: Surrender is not a clean exit — the run-off obligation and policyholder-continuity evidence mean the MGA carries responsibility until the book is properly transitioned.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Prior written approval; run-off plan required

regulation_content.regulation_text:
31. Power to issue subsidiary instructions – The Competent Authority may issue subsidiary instructions for the
following purposes, namely: –
(1) clarifying the ambiguity of the provisions of this regulation, if any; and
(2) laying down any procedural requirement ancillary to this regulation.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Lets the Authority issue subsidiary instructions to clarify any ambiguity in the regulations and to lay down procedural requirements ancillary to them.
regulation_content.practical_point: Operational procedures may sit outside the Regulations through subsidiary instructions.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Monitor IFSCA instructions and map them into the compliance register.

regulation_content.provision_heading: Power to remove difficulties and relax strict enforcement of the regulations
regulation_content.regulation_text:
32. Power to remove difficulties and relax strict enforcement of the regulations-
(1) The Competent Authority, for reasons to be recorded in writing, may in the interest of development of
insurance ecosystem in International Financial Services Centre, relax the strict enforcement of any
provision of these regulations.
(2) For seeking relaxation under sub-regulation (1), an application giving details and the grounds on which
such relaxation is being sought, shall be filed with the Competent Authority along with such non-
refundable fee as may be specified by the Authority.
(3) The application made under sub-regulation (2), complete in all respects, shall be processed within sixty
(60) days from the date of its receipt, or receipt of the responses to the clarifications sought by the
Competent Authority, if any.
(4) The Competent Authority shall dispose of the application received under sub-regulation (2), by
recording the reasons in writing for acceptance or refusal of relaxations sought by the applicant.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Gives the Authority power to relax strict enforcement of any provision, for reasons recorded in writing, in the interest of developing the IFSC insurance ecosystem. A relaxation application, with grounds and any non-refundable fee, is processed within 60 days of a complete application or of the response to clarifications sought.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: A relaxation is discretionary and reasoned — not a right. Practitioners should frame the application around ecosystem-development grounds the Authority is empowered to weigh, not around the applicant's convenience, and should expect the 60-day clock to reset if clarifications are sought.
regulation_content.practical_point: Relaxation is discretionary and should not be treated as an automatic waiver.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Keep the substantive requirement intact unless written relaxation is granted.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Relaxation processed within 60 days

regulation_content.regulation_text:
33. Power to Inspect and Investigate - The Competent Authority shall have the power to inspect the financial
statements, relevant documents and premises of the MGA at any time without prior notice, and may call for
any information from the MGA or the Applicant, so far as it relates to its activities as MGA.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The Authority may inspect the MGA's financial statements, documents and premises at any time without prior notice, and call for any information relating to its MGA activities.
regulation_content.practical_point: Inspection readiness should be maintained continuously.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain a central inspection file and nominate an internal response team.
regulation_content.risk_point: 'Without prior notice' means inspection readiness is a standing state, not a project. Records under Reg 23 and the Schedule-II retention policy must be retrievable on the day the Authority arrives.

regulation_content.provision_heading: Action in case of default and manner of suspension or cancellation of Certificate of Registration
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Lists the default grounds — nineteen in all — on which the Authority may, after due notice and a hearing, act against an MGA up to suspension or cancellation. They span breach of law, non-cooperation, false information, failure on returns, unresolved complaints, rebating, misconduct, capital/net-worth/deposit failure, MLM, BAA breach, failure to commence within 180 days, and fraud. The Authority may also act if the MGA's operations are contrary to the IFSC insurance ecosystem's interests, and may take further action under the Act and Insurance Act 1938.
regulation_content.practical_point: The grounds cover both substantive breaches and failures of governance, cooperation and financial maintenance.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain a breach register and escalation process so defaults are identified early.
regulation_content.risk_point: Any single ground suffices; the Authority need not show a pattern. Because grounds cross-refer to capital (Reg 13), deposit (Reg 15), BAA (Reg 20) and commencement (Reg 9), a breach flagged in inspection under those sections lands directly here as a cancellation trigger.
regulation_content.interview_point: List the enforcement grounds under Reg 34 that map to a failure to maintain a financial threshold, and identify which sections create those thresholds.
regulation_content.important_numbers: 19 enumerated default grounds; action after notice and hearing

regulation_content.provision_heading: Manner of holding enquiry for suspension or cancellation of Certificate of Registration
regulation_content.regulation_text:
35. Manner of holding enquiry for suspension or cancellation of Certificate of Registration—
(1) The certificate of registration of an MGA shall not be suspended or cancelled unless an enquiry has been
conducted in accordance with the procedure specified in this regulation.
(2) For the purpose of holding an enquiry under this regulation, the Competent Authority may appoint an
enquiry officer within fifteen (15) days of the initiation of the proceedings;
(3) The enquiry officer shall issue a notice to the MGA electronically or at the registered office or the
principal place of business of the MGA, calling for all data, documents or information as deemed
necessary to conduct the enquiry;
(4) An MGA may, within twenty-one (21) days from the date of receipt of such notice, furnish to the
enquiry officer a reply to the notice together with copies of documentary or other evidence relied on by
them or sought by the enquiry officer.
(5) The enquiry officer shall give a reasonable opportunity of hearing to an MGA to enable it to make
submissions in support of its reply made under sub-regulation (4) above.
(6) An MGA may either appear in person to present their case.
(7) If it is considered necessary, the enquiry officer may –
(a) require the Competent Authority to present its case through one of its officers;
(b) call for feedback/information from the foreign insurer or any other related entity during the course of
enquiry;
(c) call for additional data, documents or information from an MGA.
(8) The enquiry officer shall make all necessary efforts to complete the proceeding at the earliest but in no
case beyond sixty (60) days of the commencement of the enquiry;
Provided that in case the enquiry cannot be completed within the specified time limit of sixty (60) days
as mentioned above; the enquiry officer may seek additional time from the Competent Authority stating
the reason thereof.
(9) The enquiry officer shall, after taking into account all relevant facts and submissions made by the MGA,
submit a report to the Competent Authority within thirty (30) days of the completion of the enquiry
proceedings.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Sets the enquiry procedure before suspension or cancellation: an enquiry officer appointed within 15 days of initiation, a notice to the MGA, a 21-day window to reply with evidence, a reasonable hearing, an enquiry completed within 60 days (extendable for reasons), and a report to the Authority within 30 days of completion.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: These timelines are natural-justice guardrails. An MGA facing enquiry should calendar every one of them — the 21-day reply window in particular — because the later stages (Reg 36) allow the Authority to proceed ex parte if the MGA lets a deadline lapse.
regulation_content.practical_point: The procedure gives the MGA a formal opportunity to respond to allegations and evidence.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Preserve notices, submissions, evidence and hearing records in a dedicated enforcement file.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Enquiry officer within 15 days; MGA reply within 21 days; enquiry within 60 days; report within 30 days

regulation_content.provision_heading: Action to be taken after the receipt of the enquiry report
regulation_content.regulation_text:
36. Action to be taken after the receipt of the enquiry report –
(1) On receipt of the report from the enquiry officer, the Competent Authority shall consider the report and
issue a show-cause notice (SCN) to the MGA if the contents of the report warrant a suspension or
cancellation of the registration granted to them.
(2) The MGA shall, within twenty-one (21) days of the date of receipt of the SCN, send a reply to the
Competent Authority.
(3) The Competent Authority, after considering the reply to SCN shall pass such an order as it deems fit;
Provided that where the MGA on serving of the notice under this regulation fails to furnish any reply
within the stated period, the Competent Authority may after the expiry of such time proceed to decide
the case on merit and pass such an order as it deems fit.
(4) The Competent Authority shall send a final order made under sub-regulation (3) to the MGA.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: After the enquiry report, the Authority considers it and, if it warrants suspension or cancellation, issues a show-cause notice. The MGA replies within 21 days; the Authority then passes a reasoned order, and may proceed to decide on merits if the MGA fails to reply in time.
regulation_content.practical_point: The SCN stage is separate from the earlier enquiry and should be handled as a formal response process.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Track the 21-day SCN deadline and management/Board approvals for the response.
regulation_content.risk_point: The ex parte risk is real — a missed 21-day SCN reply lets the Authority decide on the existing record. Silence is treated as forfeiting the defence, not as buying time.
regulation_content.important_numbers: SCN reply within 21 days

regulation_content.provision_heading: Suspension or cancellation of Certificate of Registration and effects thereon
regulation_content.regulation_text:
37. Suspension or cancellation of Certificate of Registration and effects thereon—
(1) The Competent Authority shall issue the final order for suspension or cancellation of the certificate of
registration of the MGA, and it shall cease to act as an MGA from the date of the final order;
Provided that, an MGA whose certificate of registration has been suspended or cancelled shall continue
to service the contracts already concluded through it for a period of six months, within which it shall
make suitable arrangements for having the existing contracts attended to by another MGA registered
under these regulations.
(2) The Competent Authority on suspension or cancellation of certificate of registration may pass such
order as it thinks fit for the disposal of the deposit of the MGA made under regulation 15 of these
regulations.
(3) An MGA who agrees to take over the obligations of policy service from the MGA whose certificate of
registration is suspended or cancelled, shall submit its request to the foreign insurer for serving the
policies / contracts throughout the policy term.
(4) An MGA, upon obtaining the approval from the foreign insurer in terms of sub-regulation (3), can
collect remuneration on subsisting contracts with prospective effect from the date of service of the
contracts.
(5) The foreign insurer shall pay remuneration / policy service on subsisting contracts with prospective
effect from the date of allotment of service of the contracts to the new MGA with whom the foreign
insurer had executed a new BAA.
regulation_content.simple_explanation: On a final suspension/cancellation order the MGA stops acting as an MGA from the order date, but must keep servicing already-concluded contracts for six months while arranging their transfer to another registered MGA. The Authority may deal with the deposit under Reg 15, and the run-off/remuneration mechanics for the successor MGA are set out.
regulation_content.practical_point: Existing policyholder servicing does not simply stop on the date of suspension/cancellation.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain a contingency run-off/transfer plan with the foreign insurer.
regulation_content.risk_point: The six-month servicing duty survives cancellation — the MGA cannot walk away from live policyholders on the order date. Continuity of policyholder service is the object the run-off provisions protect.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Cease on order date; six-month servicing/run-off of existing contracts

regulation_content.provision_heading: Publication of order of suspension or cancellation
regulation_content.regulation_text:
38. Publication of order of suspension or cancellation —
